question: Why shouldn’t that worry me?

answer_md:
🐾 Here’s how Matt describes his leadership: empathy, clarity, and modern engineering rigor.

The engineering teams he inherited were often “over-processed, under-trusted, waiting for permission instead of owning outcomes.” At the Cloud Innovation Center, which he led at a scale of **150 people**, he worked to remove those barriers: make intent explicit, push decisions to the people closest to the work, and coach teams to think clearly rather than just execute tasks.

His “permit to fail” approach addressed teams’ fear of blame. Matt organized non-punitive post-mortems, emphasized lessons rather than finger-pointing, and supported low-stakes experiments with structured hypotheses and controlled iterations. In product incubation, he set expectations that early prototypes and user tests would often fail. Teams used those results to change product direction before committing to costly builds.

He also assembled balanced teams of engineers, product managers, and UX architects with equal participation and shared accountability. Pair programming, collaborative coding, retrospectives, and direct feedback were part of daily work, rather than relying on handoffs between separate functions.

At **Norfolk Southern**, that approach included taking ownership when defects rose despite near-complete test coverage. Matt acknowledged the failure in front of the client and **Accenture** account leadership instead of defending the dashboard. He audited the code and tests, exposed vague backlog stories, and brought in TDD experts for hands-on coaching through an “I do, we do, you do” progression.

The client stopped finding defects the dashboard could not see. Across his Cloud Innovation Center leadership work, teams achieved **4x delivery acceleration** once they embraced lean product and modern engineering practices.

question: What’s his leadership style?

answer_md:
🐾 There’s an example where Matt’s “permit to fail” philosophy did not protect a team member from the consequences of a systemic failure.

On a global platform modernization for a financial services client, Matt was the technical lead responsible for ensuring a safe environment setup. The program was under delivery pressure, with offshore teams executing test cycles across development, QA, UAT, and production. He relied on inherited environment documentation rather than verifying that IAM controls, environment boundaries, and downstream access configurations were correct.

Matt focused on delivery pressures instead of validating access patterns. He did not audit who could trigger downstream email jobs, implement compensating controls such as data masking or email interception, or verify whether production customer data had been scrubbed from downstream environments.

An offshore tester accidentally triggered an email job in UAT. Communications containing unmasked production customer data went to **thousands of real clients**.

Matt took accountability and led the team through root cause analysis and remediation. But the client demanded that the tester be removed from the project. In Matt’s words, it was “a systemic failure that resulted in an individual consequence.” Taking accountability afterward did not prevent that consequence.

The changes Matt identifies are specific: IAM validation, environment verification, PII scrubbing, and risk ownership became day-one leadership responsibilities in his delivery approach. His account of the failure is explicit: these were “assumptions [he] should have verified rather than inherited.”

question: What’s his leadership style?

answer_md:
🐾 Found it!

At **Norfolk Southern**, Matt’s initial rollout of balanced teams, pair programming, and test-driven development did not prevent a quality crisis. Those practices were in place from the start, but a couple of months into the engagement, the client reported rising defects while the dashboards showed near-complete test coverage. The credibility hit landed in front of both the client and **Accenture** account leadership.

Matt had not reinforced and verified the practices enough. An engineer was building from his own interpretation rather than the backlog story, then writing tests after the code. The backlog also contained vague stories without defined scenarios or a definition of done. Coverage looked complete, but defects went undetected.

Matt took ownership publicly and audited the codebase and test suite rather than defending the metrics. He rebuilt the backlog with SMART, testable stories and brought in frontend and backend TDD experts to work alongside the team and redo code and tests.

He then changed the daily workflow rather than relying on training alone. Test cases became a discrete step before engineering the solution, completed inside rotating pairs and checked at stand-up. New engineers paired with seasoned practitioners. Stories entered sprints only when testable, with defined scenarios and a definition of done.

The client stopped finding defects the dashboard could not see, and the failure mode did not recur after the experts left. Matt’s stated lesson was that implementing a practice is the easy half: reinforcement, follow-up, and verification had been missing.

Starting with diabetes management, Matt led an initiative to add AI-powered capabilities to the existing application rather than build a standalone demonstration.

He designed and implemented a data lake, machine learning pipeline, LLM instance, and full-stack components to process data from electronic medical records, glucometers, activity trackers, and other devices. Patients received personalized daily recommendations, medication reminders, and AI-driven guidance through a mobile app. Matt also trained healthcare teams to interpret AI-generated insights and incorporate them into treatment plans.

Alongside delivery, the CIO raised concerns about HIPAA compliance and patient privacy. Matt brought together legal, compliance, IT security, data science, and clinical representatives. He operationalized Accenture’s Responsible AI Framework through anonymization, encryption, differential privacy, access policies, and continuous monitoring and auditing.

The team delivered a working MVP in **16 weeks**, built as an extensible foundation rather than a throwaway proof of concept. Clinical teams adopted AI-generated insights into treatment planning, and the pilot maintained full HIPAA compliance. The executive team approved consideration of broader AI implementation.

answer_md:
🐾 Here’s a time Matt failed—and what happened afterward.

Matt was the tech lead on a global platform modernization delivery for a financial services client. The program was under delivery pressure, with offshore teams running test cycles across development, QA, UAT, and production. IAM controls, environment segregation, and downstream access configurations had been inherited from prior phases, along with existing documentation.

Matt was responsible for ensuring a safe environment setup. He relied on that documentation rather than verifying the configuration. He did not audit who could trigger downstream jobs or email processes, confirm that production customer data had been scrubbed, or implement compensating controls such as data masking and email interception.

An offshore tester accidentally triggered an email job in UAT. It sent communications containing unmasked production customer data to **thousands of real clients**.

Matt took accountability and led the team through root cause analysis and remediation. They identified insufficient IAM checks, unclear environment boundaries, and production data that had not been scrubbed from downstream environments. Rather than treating the incident solely as a tester’s mistake, he worked collectively with the team to understand what happened and implement corrective controls.

The client nevertheless demanded that the tester be removed from the project—a systemic failure with an individual consequence.

Matt’s stated lesson was that “assumptions are risks in disguise.” IAM validation, environment verification, PII scrubbing, and risk ownership became day-one responsibilities in his delivery approach, rather than inherited conditions he assumed were already correct.

Revised cutoff processes reduced wire-transfer delays, and training materials equipped clients to manage multi-currency accounts without ongoing support dependency.

At **American Express**, adoption of the Virtual Payments Platform lagged because clients lacked SDKs, clear documentation, and a sandbox. Matt co-created a developer portal, developed Java, .NET, and Python SDKs, and built secure, virtualized testing environments. He used Lean Product and XP practices and conducted a Client Onboarding Test Drive. Onboarding time fell, API trial usage increased within **3 months**, and the team exceeded its delivery commitment by **over 261 story points** of customer-focused value.

question: What’s his leadership style?

answer_md:
🐾 Here’s an example from **Norfolk Southern**.

In **2020**, during the Cloud Innovation Center’s first major engagement, Matt’s team was modernizing the client’s legacy Revenue and Shipment Planning platform. A couple of months in, as the pandemic forced everyone into remote work, the client reported rising defects. The dashboards showed near-complete test coverage. The concerns landed in front of both the client and **Accenture** account leadership.

Matt took ownership of the failure rather than defending the metrics. He ran a bottom-up audit of the codebase and test suite and shared the gaps openly. An engineer had been working from his own interpretation instead of the backlog story, then writing tests after the code. The backlog was also part of the problem: vague stories lacked defined scenarios and a definition of done.

Matt rebuilt the backlog with SMART, testable stories. He brought in frontend and backend test-driven development experts from Columbus to work alongside the team and redo the code and test cases properly.

For engineers, the correction included hands-on support: boot camps, coding katas, practice learning sessions, lunch and learns, and pairing with subject-matter experts through an “I do, we do, you do” progression. Product managers received product management and SMART story training, and Matt restructured agile ceremonies to keep them connected with developers and stakeholders.

Defect rates dropped as story quality and test-first discipline took hold. The client stopped finding defects the dashboard could not see, and confidence was restored through the open audit and visible improvement.

answer_md:
🐾 Here’s how Matt built the organization.

The documented CIC starting point was a **10-person pilot**, rather than **4**, growing to **150+ practitioners** across engineering, architecture, product, and design in Atlanta and Tampa. At **Accenture**, the challenge was not simply hiring: many new joiners lacked hands-on cloud-native or Agile experience, while clients needed teams ready to deliver. Matt also kept the organization deliberately flat, without managers sitting on daily delivery teams.

He built a hiring engine across **4** channels: internal bench searches, campus recruiting, contract-to-hire, and approved job requisitions. Georgia Tech recruiting, hackathons, and job fairs expanded the talent pipeline. Instead of relying only on interviews, engineers completed hands-on TDD pairing auditions; product managers and designers worked through live scoping exercises. Interviewers recorded independent votes, and a failed pairing audition ended the candidacy. Matt held the closing interview and made every final hiring decision. During scaling pushes, the process produced **4 to 6 net-new practitioners per week**, with interviewer participation capped at **2 slots per week** to protect delivery.

New hires progressed through structured enablement and round-robin pairing with seasoned practitioners. The learning model was “I do, we do, you do,” moving people from guided to independent delivery. Teams practiced pair programming, TDD, continuous delivery, user research, and Build-Measure-Learn cycles. Weekly peer-led demos, mentoring, skills matrices, and career frameworks continued development beyond onboarding.

Matt ran the organization through **11 to 13** practice and client leads. Experienced engineers served as team anchors rather than another management layer. Monday allocation reviews matched practitioners to engagements and learning work. Because managers did not observe daily delivery, evaluations drew on evidence from recent pairing partners, product managers, and anchors, rather than visibility to a boss.

Over **4 years**, the organization reached **150+ practitioners**, with near-zero attrition in the first **2 years**. CIC delivery results included **4X faster velocity** and **zero-defect deployments**, with **10-person** balanced teams delivering equivalent output to traditional **20-person** teams.

🐾 Matt’s payments work includes payment-engine delivery, legacy-system consolidation, cross-border workflow design, and developer integration.

At **JP Morgan Chase**, the ACCESS Next Generation portal needed capabilities beyond Bottomline Technologies’ WebSeries platform. Different payment types required distinct formatting, validation, compliance, and approval workflows for **135,000+ clients** across **180+ countries**. Matt served as Technology Delivery Lead, managing a blended team of **40+** across **Accenture** and bank resources in the US, Mumbai, and Bangalore.

He designed and delivered bespoke ACH, wire, FX/cross-border, and tax-payment modules. The work included NACHA file validation, integration with the bank’s foreign exchange engine, Message Authentication Code security, and payment-type-specific permissions. A user could, for example, be authorized to approve wires but not initiate FX payments. He also incorporated risk-based transaction restrictions and sanctions screening into payment flows. Alongside the engine build, Matt led payments-data migration from regional legacy systems, preserving client configurations, entitlements, transaction histories, and compliance traceability. ACCESS launched in **April 2011**; the migration completed without disruption to live payment operations.

At **RBC**, fragmented systems and manual processes delayed cross-border and bulk payments. Matt designed workflows from initiation through settlement and reconciliation, including real-time FX integration, automated alerts, recurring payments, and batch processing. The output was an implementation blueprint ready for development execution. Revised payment cutoff processes also reduced wire-transfer delays.

At **American Express**, adoption of its Virtual Payments Platform was slowed by missing SDKs, fragmented documentation, downstream dependencies, and no sandbox. Matt led developer-portal work that included cross-stack SDKs, use-case-driven documentation, and secure virtualized testing environments, letting clients explore and test without waiting on downstream systems. His team used Lean Product and XP practices and validated the portal through a Client Onboarding Test Drive. API consumption and trial usage increased within **3 months** of relaunch; onboarding time fell, and the team exceeded its delivery commitment by over **261 story points**.

answer_md:
🐾 Tracking this down...

At **JP Morgan Chase**, Matt worked on ACCESS Next Generation, a corporate banking portal serving **135,000+ clients** across **180+ countries**. Bottomline Technologies’ WebSeries platform provided the foundation, but its out-of-box capabilities did not cover the bank’s payment formatting, validation, compliance, and workflow requirements. Meanwhile, regional legacy systems had different data models, client configurations, and entitlement structures.

As Technology Delivery Lead, Matt managed a blended team of **40+** across **Accenture** and bank resources in Mumbai, Bangalore, and the US. Rather than treating ACCESS as a standard vendor deployment, he managed the build-versus-configure boundary and designed and delivered bespoke ACH, wire, FX/cross-border, and federal tax payment modules. He spent **70 to 80%** of his time embedded at Bottomline’s Portsmouth offices.

The engineering included NACHA file validation, Message Authentication Code payment verification, and payment-type-specific permissions, such as allowing wire approval without FX initiation. His team integrated transaction monitoring, risk-based approval controls, and sanctions screening into payment workflows. Matt also led the payments data migration, preserving client configurations, transaction histories, and compliance traceability without disrupting live payment operations. ACCESS launched in **April 2011**.

At **RBC**, he designed cross-border payment workflows from initiation through settlement and reconciliation. Working with the FX team, he defined real-time currency conversion integration points, automated alerts, batch processing, and revised payment cutoff processes. The deliverable was a complete implementation blueprint, not a claimed production platform launch.

At **American Express**, the problem was adoption of its Virtual Payments Platform: missing SDKs, fragmented documentation, downstream dependencies, and no sandbox. Matt’s work combined Java, .NET, and Python SDKs with use-case-driven documentation, a secure sandbox, and virtualized testing environments. The team used Discovery and Framing workshops, Lean Product and XP practices, and a Client Onboarding Test Drive. API trial usage increased within **3 months**, onboarding time fell, and the team exceeded its delivery commitment by over **261 story points**.

Matt was brought in roughly seven months into **Fiserv**'s 14-month, **$8.5M** white-label card portal program, the shared platform behind branded credit card sites for **2M+** cardholders across **15** financial institutions. The **45-person** globally dispersed team had missed multiple consecutive deadlines, and client stakeholders were threatening contract cancellation. He recovered a Q4 release that was **3 weeks** behind, avoiding **$500K** in penalties, and the program was delivered **3%** under budget with zero critical defects at launch.

Want to hear how he moved that team from 6-month waterfall releases to 2-week sprints?

🐾 Here’s how Matt changed the working model.

At **Fiserv**, the **45-person** team was working through **6-month** waterfall release cycles, with requirements buried in a **200-page** business requirements document organized by system modules. Developers in India, testers in the Philippines, and designers in Ireland had no visibility into work status. Multiple deadlines had slipped, stakeholders were threatening contract cancellation, and PMO and compliance teams resisted agile delivery.

Matt changed how work was defined—not just the meeting schedule. He decomposed the requirements into persona-based user stories and rebuilt JIRA from a single To Do/Done board into a multi-tiered Kanban/Scrum architecture. The program’s **47** acceptance criteria became Epics, with stories moving through specific workflow columns. He established follow-the-sun handoffs: a **7 AM CST** scrum-of-scrums and **11 PM CST** synchronization.

Instead of waiting until month **6** to discover branding, interface, or accessibility problems, Matt introduced biweekly sprint demos for **Fiserv** stakeholders. When reviewers lacked bandwidth, he negotiated dedicated review windows. He maintained existing steering committee reporting while adding sprint-level visibility.

For compliance, Matt used JIRA as the system of record, with audit trails, attached ADA scans, and developer comments rather than static Word documents. He also trained offshore teams on JAWS/NVDA screen-reader audits and included those checks in the Definition of Done. Alongside those changes, he introduced mandatory code reviews, unit tests, and automated build quality gates.

The team moved to **2-week** sprints within **3 months**. JIRA gave **50+** stakeholders across **3** time zones real-time visibility, and PMO and compliance accepted it as the system of record. Sprint demos caught branding and ADA issues early rather than at month **6**.

🐾 Here’s the story of Matt’s work at **Norfolk Southern**.

Matt led the Cloud Innovation Center’s first engagement: modernizing the railroad’s Revenue and Shipment Planning platform without stopping the railroad. Its mainframe dated to the **1970s**. Orders could fall out unnoticed until customers called, business rules lived in COBOL and assembly maintained by a shrinking workforce, and clerks manually worked through waybill and rating fallout on green-screen consoles. The client was accustomed to mainframe thinking, account leadership to waterfall delivery, and Matt’s team was learning a new working model as the pandemic forced remote work.

He kept the mainframe as the system of record while building APIs, microservices, and CockroachDB alongside it. Event storming, the Boris Exercise, and SNAP-E documentation mapped business domains, data flows, dependencies, and risks. Change data capture synchronized the platforms; reconciliation checked that nothing was lost. When the client grew restless for tangible progress, Matt brought its revenue management team into the innovation hub to co-create the Shipper Revenue System workspace through weekly build-measure-learn iterations.

The engagement also hit a quality crisis: defects were rising despite near-complete test coverage. Matt took ownership, audited the code and tests, and found tests written after code and backlog stories without clear scenarios. He rebuilt testable stories, brought in TDD coaches, and reinforced test-first work through rotating pairs. A **2-day** CIC Academy course ran twice monthly over **6 months**. Pairing spread scarce legacy knowledge and let client engineers learn Angular, Node, Spring Boot, and cloud-native development while building the application.

The MVP launched covering **95%** of targeted use cases. Billing clerks and shippers could audit malformed waybill data before downstream pricing errors. EDI validation shifted fallout detection from customer complaints to proactive trading-partner notifications. The client stopped finding defects the dashboard could not see, and its contributors gained the skills to support and manage the new application after **Accenture** rolled off.
